The instructor is one of the best I've had so far. His approach to teaching a course, which is simply great, is unfortunately unparalleled here at Bilkent. This was the most interactive course I've taken in my entire education, and I'm doubtful anything will come close in the future. You get participation points every single lecture, and the instructor does write your name down every time you raise your hand. This was actually nice as it did succeed to encourage participation in most people present. The instructor also doesn't have an authoritarian attitude towards students, so you can come to class and almost act as if you're conversing on psychology with a friend. Thanks to all of these upsides, which no doubt were specific to this instructor and do not apply to all sections of this course, this was actually my most enjoyable course this term and I'm thankful to Kaan Kerman for that. On the other hand, if you're someone who just likes to come to class, sit down, listen and leave, you're probably better off in another section.

His strengths lie in his good practical understanding of the course material and his ability to effectively explain key concepts with real life examples. However, his strength in course topic fall short because of his weaknesses. All below are my personal opinions and one may want to consider or not, He lack classroom management and his manner of communication with the students does not align well with the expectations of a university setting, considering that we are all adults. Every time i was in clss, I felt like i went back to high school days. I was expecting more from a uni level stat course. His greatest weakness comes from a very poorly thought of course organization. I find it important to mention that, he brought an unexpected mid-semester attendance policy that was not mentioned in the syllabus at all, and counted the attendance as one question from the final. I find this to be quite problematic considering he made the unexpected attendance limit so high that because it was mid semester and half the classes were complete almost all students lost points if they missed even a single class. To continue, the 6 midterms conduced had a really poor question to point ratio where only 2 questions correspond to 5 points (which is literally a letter grade interval). Thus, our letter grades depended on only 2 questions that was randomly selected from a huge chapter of information. If he was determined to do these "midterms", he could've simply take the time to include more questions in them that we wouldn't have needed to risk a whole letter grade in every single 6 "midterms" if we only missed 2 questions. 
To sum up despite his strong practical understanding of the material; his poor communication, not well managed classes and unbalanced point practices made the course turn very empty and below university-level expectations which ultimately undermining both trust and the learning experience of such an important course. I wouldn't recommend future course takers.

The instructor teaches the class as if it was an oral exam. His style is asking questions about the topic that will be covered at that particular class session. He gives reading homework prior to the class and asks questions about the topics we were ought to read during the class session. As me and most of my classmates have agreed this term, this is highly ineffective. Encouraging in-class participation is a good method for having students express ideas, however, I believe for this course in-class participation is the top priority rather than teaching us the concepts. For example, when I ask a question, the teacher turns this question to an in-class participation opportunity for other students, and has other students explain to me rather than doing it himself. Each week, we were supposed to participate at least once, so eventually, I stopped trying to learn from the classes and just went to the class to get my compulsory participation point and leave at the second hour of the class. I felt no interest in the class because I couldn't see active teaching other than asking questions to students. Also, the course topics were much larger at the beginning of the semester and he could manage to cover many topics till the end of the semester. I think anyone who will take this class from Mr. Kerman should consider that their in-class participation is the top priority of this class.
